facts.statement: The only well-known species, P. anglicus, was a fish approximately 25 cm long.
facts.quote: The only species known in any detail, P. anglicus was a fish about 25 cm long.

facts.statement: Fossils of Ptomacanthus are primarily found in the Old Red Sandstone formations of the United Kingdom.
facts.quote: Ptomacanthus is known mainly from the Old Red Sandstone of the United Kingdom.

facts.statement: Two indeterminate species of Ptomacanthus are known from shoulder-girdle fossils found in Castle Mattock Quarry, Herefordshire, and Zaleszychi, Ukraine.
facts.quote: Two indeterminate species are known from shoulder-girdles recovered from Castle Mattock Quarry, Herefordshire and Zaleszychi, Ukraine.

facts.statement: P. anglicus is significant for understanding early vertebrate evolution because it preserves a scientifically informative portion of the braincase.
facts.quote: P. anglicus is important to our understanding of early vertebrate evolution as it preserves part of the braincase, a scientifically informative part of the skeleton.

facts.statement: Due to the rare preservation of acanthodian skeletons, the braincase of Ptomacanthus is only the second such braincase known to science.
facts.quote: Because of the cartilaginous makeup of the acanthodian internal skeleton, it is very rarely preserved, and the braincase of Ptomacanthus is only the second acanthodian braincase known to science (the first being that of Acanthodes).

facts.statement: Ptomacanthus lived during the Lochkovian stage, between 419.62 and 413.02 million years ago.
facts.quote: Time range: Lochkovian to Lochkovian (419.62 to 413.02 million years ago)

facts.statement: Ptomacanthus is classified within the parent group Chondrichthyes.
Ptomacanthus belongs to the class Chondrichthyes.
The discovery of the Ptomacanthus braincase reignited scientific debate regarding the evolutionary relationships of acanthodians and early vertebrates.
facts.quote: The description of this braincase reignited debate over the relationships of acanthodians as well as those of early vertebrates more generally.

rejected.statement: Ptomacanthus, meaning thorny corpse, is an extinct genus of spiny sharks that are early relatives of modern cartilaginous fishes.
rejected.quote: Ptomacanthus (meaning thorny corpse) is an extinct genus of spiny shark, an early relative of living cartilaginous fishes (sharks, rays, and chimaeras).

rejected.quote: Like other acanthodians it had small, shark like scales, and a suite of fin-spines in front of its dorsal, pectoral, and pelvic fins.
